title: Investment Calculator
text: I’ve been working on building a better investment calculator to enable myself and others to get a better idea of where they need to be in order to reach their retirement goals. To be sure, this isn’t fully fleshed out so you can see different accounts or assign different rates to different pools of money. That said, what this calculator allows you to do which is distinct from other basic investment calculators like the ones offered by Nerdwallet or Bankrate is that you can input different rates of return. Here, a “bear” case is an undesirable rate of return whereas a “base” case is likely and a “bull” case is optimistic.

title: MA Property Tax
text:
If you spend enough time with homeowners, you’re likely to hear them gripe about property taxes. And as you’d expect, the volume of griping increases with an increase in the amount of property taxes paid.
But even if you’re not a homeowner, property taxes are a big deal. If you’re home shopping, along with principal, interest, and private mortgage insurance, it’s one of the four biggest line items in your estimated mortgage payment. Perhaps more importantly, as a resident of whatever municipality, property taxes are often the largest contributor of revenue.
The questions of who to tax, at what rate, and for what purpose are at the core local, state, and national politics. In my own town, the local paper has been filled with news and commentary regarding funding for local schools, the poor quality of roads, and the budget more generally. It’s even a flashpoint in this year’s municipal election.
In an effort to ground public conversation in data, I wanted to build a usable tool for folks to look at property tax rates across time and space. The interactive tables and graphics below aim to do just that.


Data for property tax rate for Massachusetts municipalities can be found here and the data for municipality geometry can be found here

title: MA Property Tax
text:
But What are property taxes?
Property taxes are tied to the value of a home and are paid by the homeowner. In Massachusetts, The total amount paid is a function of the assessed value of a home and the property tax rate. It’s important to note that the assessed value of a home is not the same as the cost of the home. For example, in California, property taxes are largely a function of the purchasing price and rate. But in Massachusetts, the purchasing price of a home and its assessed value are distinct with the assessed value often being lower than the purchasing price.
Why the discrepancy between assessed value and purchase price? The major reason in Massachusetts is tied to the passage of Proposition 2 1/2 which passed in 1980 and went into effect in 1982. The state provides a number of YouTube videos(!) that explain the proposition and its effects. There’s also a not-so-easy to follow primer. That said, the TLDR is that it limited the annual increase in property tax revenue municipalities could levy by 2.5%. For example, if my town of Northampton raised $1,000,000 in property tax revenue, the max it could raise the following year would be $1,025,000. There are exceptions for new growth and overrides but that’s the jist.

section: Visualizing Rates Across Massachusetts in the Current Fiscal Year
text:
Visualizing Rates Across Massachusetts in the Current Fiscal Year
The map below highlights rates across all municipalities in the state of Massachusetts. The lighter the color, the lower the rate.


show code
# path to data
data_path <- "../../../Library/CloudStorage/GoogleDrive-pezeshka@gmail.com/My Drive/R/interests_github/data/"

# read in property tax data with geo. Saved as R file
tax_prop <- read_rds(file = paste0(data_path, "clean_tax_geo_data.R"))

# read in geometry data for the municipalities
library(sf)
map_sf <- st_read(paste0(data_path, "clean_ma_geo.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)

fig <- 
  plot_ly(
    map_sf,
    split = ~municipality,
    color = ~residential,            # fill color by rate
    showlegend = FALSE,
    stroke = I("white"),             # Set the border color
    span = I(0.3),                   # Set the border width
    text = ~paste0(                  # Define hover text
      "<b>", municipality, "</b><br>",
      "Residential Tax Rate: $", round(residential, 2), "</b><br>",
      "County: ", county
    ),
    hoverinfo = "text",
    hoveron = "fills"
  ) %>%
  hide_colorbar() %>%
  layout(
    title = "2025 Residential Property Tax Rates by Municipality<br>Per $1,000 in Assessed Value",
    geo = list(visible = FALSE)
  )

fig

title: MA Property Tax
text:
Property Tax Rates Over Time
Below I’ve visualized Property Tax Rates over time. The filters below allow you to choose one or more municipalities or counties. You can also narrow the time range by using the slider filter for year. By default the municipality filter is set to Northampton with the county blank and showing all available data.


show code
library(crosstalk)
# need county in tax_prop 
shared_df <- SharedData$new(tax_prop)

gg_rates <- ggplot(shared_df, aes(x = fiscal_year, y = residential, color = municipality, group = municipality)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) + 
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  labs(
    title = "Residential Property Tax Rates Over Time",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Rate per $1,000 Assessed Value",
    color = "Municipality" # Sets the legend title
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

bscols(
  widths = c(4, 4, 4), 
  filter_select(
    id = "municipality_filter", 
    label = "Select Municipality/ies", 
    sharedData = shared_df, 
    group = ~municipality, 
    multiple = TRUE, 
    all = FALSE
  ), 
  filter_select(
    id = "county_filter",
    label = "Select County or Counties:",
    sharedData = shared_df,
    group = ~county,
    multiple = TRUE,
    all = FALSE
  ), 
  filter_slider(
      id = "year_filter",
      label = "Select Year Range:",
      sharedData = shared_df,
      column = ~fiscal_year, # Filter by the 'year' column
      step = 1, # Move the slider in 1-year increments
      sep = "" # Removes the comma from thousands in year (e.g., 2,024)
    )
  )

show code
function filter_default() {
    document.getElementById("municipality_filter").getElementsByClassName("selectized") 
[0].selectize.setValue("Northampton", false);
 }
window.onload = filter_default;



Northampton’s property tax rate peaked in 2022 at $17.89 per $1,000 of assessed value following the pandemic and the dramatic rise in home prices. The rate has since dropped by ~22% with the 2025 Fiscal Year rate at $13.89.
But just because the rate drops does not mean that the total amount paid will decline. That’s because there’s a dance between assessed value and the tax rate. If the assessed value significantly climbs, keeping the rate constant might violate Proposition 2.5 (see Section 2), overrides and new construction notwithstanding.
And so down the rabbit hole we go to get a better understanding of the number of properties, the assessed value of all properties, and the how the ratio of assessed value to parcel or property counts have changed over time.

title: Investment Calculator
text:
What I’ll be adding

A ‘Financial Goal’ Input
In the FIRE community and elsewhere, you might hear about this as being Your Number. Your Number usually means the amount of money you need to retire or be financially independent. But how do you go about knowing Your Number? At the very least, you’ll want to know or estimate four things.

The annual rate of inflation
Year until you retire
Desired annual spending
A safe withdrawal rate



show code
dob <- as_date("1985-08-30") ## date of birth
retire_date <- dob %m+% years(60) # here we take dob and add 60 years to it in case you have a retirement age in mind and don't think about years to retirement
years_til_retirement <- round(time_length(interval(Sys.Date(), retire_date), unit = "years"), 0) # calculating years to retirement... long way but useful. 
inflation_rate <- 1.04 # projected inflation rate over that timespan. 

dollars_future <- round(inflation_rate^years_til_retirement, 2)
spend_retirement_today <- 150000
spend_retirement_future <- spend_retirement_today*dollars_future
portfolio_needed <- spend_retirement_future*25


Folks do this differently, but I start off with the annual rate of inflation and the number of years I have until I retire. The reason: If I know those the things, I can assign a value to what my future dollar is worth compared to now. We don’t need to go all the way into it but what inflation does is the erode the purchasing power of a dollar over time. In other words, it will take more future dollars to replace the purchase power of today’s dollar. Here’s the formula for calculating how many future dollars you’ll need to make up for one current dollar (1+ 'inflation rate') ^ 'years to retirement' = 'future dollars needed'. So if you assumed a 4% rate of inflation and you have 20 years until retirement, the formula would look like 1.04^20. If you run those numbers, you know you’ll need 2.19 in 20 years to make up the purchasing power of $1 today.
It’s important to note that The Federal Reserve’s target rate is 2%. Some crypto folks don’t believe the Fed will keep that target rate. While I tend to think folks like this are mostly full of it, I just don’t see inflation returning to that long-term target rate. And if it does? Well, that just means I’ll have more money come retirement. Not a bad problem to have.
So now that we know that you’ll need more dollars in the future to have the same purchasing power today, it’s worth spending some time thinking about how much you’d like to spend in a year to live the kind of life you’d like to live. And remember, it’s retirement. You may have fewer expenses in the future because you won’t be paying for daycare or maybe you’ll have paid off your mortgage and will only be on the hook for property taxes and insurance. Regardless, think about how much money you’d want annually today and then multiply that by the inflation multiple we identified above assuming a 4% interest rate with 20 years til retirement: 2.19. For my wife and I, our goal is to be able to spend approximately $150,000.00/year in today’s dollars in retirement which means I’d want to be able to withdraw $328,500.00 per year in retirement.
What’s left? Identifying a safe withdrawal rate. Bigger Pockets Money and ChooseFI have done a few great pockets on what a safe withdrawal rate is and how to think about it. I prefer back of the envelope math and will stick with the 4% rule which means I can effectively withdraw 4% of my portfolio per year with a very small risk of running out of money. Caveats not withstanding, this means my portfolio would need to be 25 times the size of my desired withdrawal amount or $8,212,500.00.
To be sure, that number assumes we’ll have no other income. But we will. I know folks say that Social Security is going away but as for now it looks like Social Security will have reduced rather than no benefits. Social Security estimates that it will have to reduce benefits by 23%, a far cry from being cut to 0. You can also supplement your income with investment property if you’re in that game or a part-time job. Regardless, I want this tool to help paint a picture of the trajectory you’re on to reach your finacial independece or retirement goals.
[Disclosure]: I’m new to this so please bear with me as I write and rewrite this page. Maybe I’ll turn it into a blog. I don’t know. Enjoy!
